title: The Red Fort Trials
subtitle: Bhulabhai Desai and the Last Argument of an Empire
region: Red Fort, Delhi; Bombay, Karachi and Calcutta naval establishments
moral: An empire weakens when its soldiers doubt its justice.

sources.citation: Two Historic Trials in Red Fort, Publications Division, Government of India
sources.note: Published account of INA court-martial proceedings and defence arguments.

sources.citation: National Archives of India, INA Trial Records, Home/Political Department, 1945-1946
sources.note: Primary files on charges, evidence and commutation.

sources.citation: Mithi Mukherjee, India in the Shadows of Empire (OUP, 2010)
sources.note: Recent interpretation of the trials as anti-colonial legal argument.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of Red Fort looming at dusk

dialogue.text: In 1945, in the shadow of the Red Fort, Bhulabhai Desai turned a treason trial into a mirror — and the empire saw its own armies looking back in doubt.

panels.shot: wide aerial of war-torn Asia fading into Delhi

dialogue.text: The Second World War had bled continents. In Asia, prisoners had chosen a different flag — Subhas Bose’s Azad Hind, the Indian National Army.

panels.shot: medium interior of a modest study, lamplight

dialogue.text: Far from the front, an aging barrister watched these storms. Bhulabhai Desai — veteran lawyer, Congress leader, believer in argument as weapon.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Desai reading a telegram

dialogue.text: In late 1945 a message came. Three INA officers would be tried by court-martial at the Red Fort — for waging war against the King.

panels.shot: profile medium of Desai rising from his chair

dialogue.speaker: bhulabhai_desai
dialogue.text: If law is their weapon, let us meet them in that arena.

panels.shot: epic wide of Red Fort interior courtyard

dialogue.text: In November 1945, the fort that once housed emperors became a courtroom. Shah Nawaz Khan, Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon and Prem Sahgal now stood where Mughal power had once ruled.

panels.shot: tight medium of Desai addressing the court

dialogue.text: Desai chose not to plead for mercy. He challenged the foundation: if Azad Hind was a government, could obedience to it be treason?

panels.shot: close-up on Desai’s face in mid-argument

dialogue.speaker: bhulabhai_desai
dialogue.text: When a people seek their own sovereign, is loyalty to them a crime?

panels.shot: wide shot of crowded gallery and press benches

dialogue.text: Outside the legal codes, another verdict was forming. Crowds followed every word. For many, the docked officers were not traitors — they were symbols.

panels.shot: muted montage-style wide: courtroom contrasted with streets

dialogue.text: The court weighed charges of desertion and murder. On the streets, slogans spoke of sacrifice, Bose and freedom. Law and sentiment pulled in opposite directions.

panels.shot: medium of Desai seated, exhausted, as judgment is read

dialogue.text: In the end, the court-martial followed the book. The officers were found guilty, sentenced to transportation and dismissal from service.

panels.shot: close-up on Desai’s hands clasped together

dialogue.text: On paper, Desai had lost. But the echo of his arguments carried beyond the Red Fort walls, into bazaars, mills and barracks.

panels.shot: wide shot of mass protest outside the Red Fort

dialogue.text: Protests flared across cities. The government, watching the anger and unrest, commuted the sentences. The law’s judgment remained; its punishment softened under pressure.

panels.shot: map-like aerial transitioning from Delhi to port cities

dialogue.text: But the deeper tremor lay elsewhere. In the very forces meant to guard the empire, discontent had been hardening into anger.

panels.shot: deck-level wide shot on a Royal Indian Navy ship in Bombay

dialogue.text: In February 1946, ratings of the Royal Indian Navy — poorly fed, racially slighted, war-weary — watched the INA trials and the news with growing bitterness.

panels.shot: medium shot of ratings around a mess table

dialogue.text: Food complaints mixed with politics. The trials turned abstract grievances into a shared cause. On 18 February, a strike began in Bombay.

panels.shot: dramatic wide of ships with flags and painted slogans

dialogue.text: Within days, it spread: 78 ships, 20 shore establishments from Bombay to Karachi and Calcutta. Ratings raised nationalist slogans and defied orders.

panels.shot: street-level wide of Bombay crowd watching the harbour

dialogue.text: Onshore, responses split. Some political leaders hailed their courage; others worried at the chaos of an armed mutiny.

panels.shot: interior medium of a nationalist leader in discussion

dialogue.text: Mahatma Gandhi opposed the uprising, fearing violence without discipline. Vallabhbhai Patel worked, step by step, to persuade the ratings to lay down arms.

panels.shot: somber wide of armed British troops facing a ship

dialogue.text: The empire could not ignore armed defiance in its own fleet. Guns were brought up, ultimatums given. Behind every order lay the memory of other naval mutinies.

panels.shot: medium shot of ratings lowering a flag

dialogue.text: After appeals from nationalist leaders and the threat of overwhelming force, the ratings surrendered between 22 and 23 February. Their demands unmet, their defiance recorded.

panels.shot: montage wide of courtrooms, ships, and crowds fading together

dialogue.text: Historians would later see these moments together — the INA trials, the naval revolt — as signs that the empire’s moral claim over its Indian soldiers was breaking.

panels.shot: quiet medium of an older Desai seated, reflective

dialogue.text: Bhulabhai Desai did not live to see full independence. Yet his arguments echoed in every later debate on sovereignty, loyalty and the right to resist authority.

panels.shot: slow pull-back from Desai’s silhouette against the Red Fort

dialogue.text: An empire weakens when those who guard it question its justice. In the Red Fort and on the seas, Bhulabhai Desai and the ratings forced that question into the open — where it still waits for every power.
